analysis.title: Strategic: Put cash to work
key_insights: UBS CIO argues that holding cash long term carries a large opportunity cost. From 1900 to 2025, USD 1 grew in real terms to USD 1.80 in Treasury bills, USD 7.50 in bonds and USD 3,296 in stocks.

Reinvestment risk: if interest rates fall over the coming years, each maturing fixed deposit may be replaced at a lower rate, which would gradually reduce income. UBS suggests a bond ladder with staggered maturities to avoid reinvesting the whole balance at one point in the rate cycle.

UBS proposes splitting cash into three buckets by time horizon. Everyday cash covers the next 12 months of spending and emergency reserves. Core liquidity covers 1-3 years. Investment cash covers money not needed for 3-5 years. Money needed beyond 5 years can go into a diversified portfolio.

For core liquidity, UBS lists fixed-term deposits, certificates of deposit, Treasury bills, short-dated government and corporate bonds, and short-duration investment grade bond funds. For investment cash it points to medium-term government and investment grade corporate bonds, accepting some price fluctuation for higher income.

UBS rates fixed income Attractive and favors quality short- and medium-maturity bonds. It is more cautious on the longest maturities because persistent fiscal deficits and heavy government bond issuance could keep long-term yields and term premiums elevated.

UBS recommends quality bonds as the first step out of cash, ahead of equities. High starting yields give an income cushion against moderate further rate rises. Bonds could also gain in price if inflation moderates, growth weakens and yields fall.

Phasing in has a cost. In S&P 500 data from 1945 to January 2025, investing immediately beat a 12-month phase-in 70% of the time. UBS presents phasing as a behavioral tool for cautious investors, not a return-maximizing one, and suggests deploying funds on a set schedule, at deposit maturities or at portfolio milestones.

Market timing: from September 1989 to October 2026, USD 100 in the S&P 500 grew to about USD 3,600 if held throughout, about USD 3,200 if the best day was missed and about USD 2,500 if the best year was missed. UBS notes that the best days often come within weeks of the worst declines.

trade_ideas.description: Move excess cash into quality short- and medium-maturity government and investment grade corporate bonds, then phase into a diversified portfolio over time. Use a bond ladder for deposit maturities.
trade_ideas.rationale: Bond yields have risen enough to restore meaningful income, and holding cash carries inflation and reinvestment risk.
trade_ideas.risk: Medium-duration bonds see larger price fluctuations. Longer maturities are exposed to elevated term premiums from fiscal deficits and heavy issuance.

risk_factors: Inflation steadily erodes the real value of cash.
Reinvestment risk if deposit rates fall.
Money market funds are investments, not deposits. Their value can fluctuate and they are not guaranteed to hold a stable value.
Persistent fiscal deficits and heavy government bond issuance could keep long-term yields and term premiums elevated.
Recent AI-led volatility in equities is unsettling risk-averse investors.
Phasing in will often underperform investing immediately, because markets have historically risen over time.

tension_points.bull_case: Investing immediately beat a 12-month phase-in 70% of the time in S&P 500 data from 1945 to January 2025, so waiting for a better entry has a substantial opportunity cost.
tension_points.bear_case: A phased plan, starting with quality fixed income, helps cautious investors avoid one large, uncomfortable decision and avoids tying the whole portfolio to equity entry timing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: UBS states no specific level or event. It says phasing will often underperform because markets have historically risen over time.

theme_stances.key_argument: The rise in bond yields has restored meaningful income potential, so quality short- and medium-maturity bonds are a more measured first step out of cash than equities.
theme_stances.evidence: We currently regard fixed income as Attractive

theme_stances.key_argument: Persistent fiscal deficits and heavy government bond issuance could keep longer-term yields and term premiums elevated.
theme_stances.evidence: We are more cautious on the longest maturities.
